passages.t: The friends fall silent, and Elihu is angry
passages.happening:
‘So these three men stopped answering Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes’ (verse 1).

‘This kindled the anger of Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram. He burned with anger against Job for justifying himself rather than God, and he burned with anger against Job’s three friends because they had failed to refute Job, and yet had condemned him’ (verses 2-3).

Elihu had waited to speak because the others were older. But when he saw that the three had no more to say, his anger flared.
passages.hearers:
Job has finished his defense and signed it, demanding that God answer. The reader expects God to speak next. Instead, a man never mentioned before steps forward. Elihu's speeches fill six chapters, and no one interrupts or answers him. Job called for God, and he gets another human voice.

These verses are the first prose since chapter 2, apart from the short headings that name each speaker. They tell what the poetry could not: the friends have stopped, and Elihu has waited because he was younger.

Elihu is introduced with a fuller family line than anyone else in the book. Buz was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and a brother of a man named Uz, the name of Job's homeland. Nothing is known of this Elihu outside the book, and he appears in neither the prologue nor the epilogue.

His anger is named four times in these verses, literally his nose burned. He is angry with Job for justifying himself rather than God, and with the friends for condemning Job without answering him.
passages.later: Elihu's family name reaches back to Abraham's kin: ‘Uz the firstborn, his brother Buz, Kemuel (the father of Aram)’ (Genesis 22:21).
passages.asks: Elihu was angry with everyone in the room. Ask whether anger has ever made you sure you were the one who saw clearly. And ask what you would have said to Job, if you had been the one listening for thirty chapters.

passages.happening:
‘So Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite declared’ (verse 6). “I am young in years, while you are old; that is why I was timid and afraid to tell you what I know. I thought that age should speak, and many years should teach wisdom. But there is a spirit in a man, the breath of the Almighty, that gives him understanding” (verses 6-8).

He has listened to all their reasoning, and no one has answered Job. They should not say they have found wisdom and that God must deal with Job. He will not answer Job with their arguments.

“For I am full of words, and my spirit within me compels me. Behold, my belly is like unvented wine; it is about to burst like a new wineskin” (verses 18-19). He must speak, and he will flatter no one.
passages.hearers:
In that world, as in most traditional societies, age went with wisdom. The elders sat at the gate and gave counsel, and the young listened first. Elihu honors that at first, and then challenges it. Understanding comes from the breath of the Almighty, ruach, which can be given to the young as well as the old.

His picture of himself comes from winemaking. New wine was kept in goatskins, and as it fermented the gas expanded; a skin with no vent could burst.

The speech is unusually full of himself: his youth, his waiting, his fullness of words, his honesty, for sixteen verses before he says anything about Job's case. Some readers find this pompous or even comic. Others see the proper courtesy of a younger man speaking to his elders.
passages.later: The prophet Joel promised the same Spirit to the young as to the old: “your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions” (Joel 2:28).
passages.hard:
Is Elihu a wise voice or another failed comforter?

Interpreters have long disagreed. Some see Elihu as a positive figure who corrects both Job and the friends and prepares the way for God's speeches. They note that he brings a new idea, that suffering can be God's discipline and warning, and that God does not rebuke him at the end; 42:7-9 names only the three friends. Others see a young man who repeats the friends' arguments at greater length. They point to his long self-introduction, his anger, and the fact that God, when he speaks, ignores Elihu entirely. Still others think his speeches were added to the book later, since he is missing from the prologue and epilogue and his style differs. A fourth view sees him as deliberately mixed, his partial truth and partial arrogance part of the book's design.

The text does not settle it, and these notes take no side. Readers should weigh his words as they would any human speaker in Job.
passages.asks: Elihu believed that understanding comes from God's Spirit, not from age. Ask whose voice you discount because of their age, young or old. And ask whether you are so full of words, as Elihu was, that you could not wait to listen.
